Got cut off 1 by 1 from self inflected management commentary.

3. Then there was no M&A announcements, and that also turned into "looking at opportunities". 
4. Lot of long-term CPO economic opportunities were redirected into near term pluggable discussions. 

I'm not sure if it's a communication or cultural issue, but the underlying business got stronger. The ambitions they initially set with press releases in H1 were cut off. 

But valuation premiums can always come back depending on communication and subsequent execution next earnings.

text:
In terms of laser industry dynamics: 

- $LITE: "Take or pay. There's a very strong commitment from the customer side, and in some cases, there's a prepay element as well". Hyperscalers were explicitly funding their capacity expansion as well

- $COHR: Upfront payments in almost every LTA, according to its CEO. 

Both Lumentum and Coherent are the gold standard in terms of financing + demand signals. 

- For Chinese laser suppliers:

Optical module makers are actively financing their supply chains (even for lower range pluggables), as seen with Cambridge. 

In terms of US supply chains: 

- $AAOI CFO gave a note: "Customer financing is more likely for emerging technologies such as CPO and NPO than conventional 800G and 1.6T transceivers."

- $AAOI got a CPO + laser contract worth $700m for 2028-2029. But resulted in more ATMs instead of funding expansion with prepayments... 

I think people can agree AOI as a business at $3.7B MC is very operationally compelling:

- since they signed a $1B-$1.5B LTA with one hyperscaler
-  $2.2B LTA all in a single quarter.

But with management repeatedly creates expectations that later disclosures contrast with, which I agree is strange. 

Lot of current financing (as seen with Neoclouds) are done with prepayments given tightening. Or if a supplier is important enough (as seen with $SPCX), they'll help refinance the company. 

So I'm really not sure what's happening with $AAOI, maybe it's overstated competitive positioning or something else.

text:
$NUAI - the main catalysts I’m watching following the latest earnings call:

1. Phase 1 tenant agreement. 
Negotiations are at an advanced stage. Management said the economics were agreed, with technical details still being finalised. A signed lease is the biggest near-term catalyst. (I'm expecting a deal similar to the one secured by $RIOT with $ANT).

2. Phase 2 air permit. 
The application has been filed, and management expected approval before the end of 2026. 

3. Phase 2 tenant agreement.

text:
I spent a little bit of time reading Lab researcher / Hyperscaler expert calls on Tegus and building an ANT model (+AI GW Model)

My conclusion is that 2027 is going to get pretty crazy.

I don’t think I wrapped my head around just how much $ANT is going to be spending on training.

Market rightfully reacted when learning how little ANT was spending on serving customers vs. training with their ~25% split. The implication when you roll fwd Compute / % mix to training is pretty eye opening.

My ANT base case is they spend ~6x more on training/RL models by end of ‘27 vs. the current / Opus 5.5 class model. When you factor in efficiency gains (esp on the RL side), it is probably closer to a 10x increase in effective training. I personally can’t fathom what that leads to.

A huge amount of the debate will come down to:
What does it mean for ANT (and not too too far behind OAI) to spend 10x more effective compute training models over the next year?

There’s a camp that believes meaningful chunks of intelligence tap out – that for something like Coding, everyone will plateau at a similar point and with not too much training / RL bc the models essentially know how to solve this problem..RSI helps you get to the plateau faster bc the models know how to solve that problem (argument from META researcher below).

I’m more bullish on the frontier and have extreme excitement about what 10x more effective compute to train models by the end of ‘27 could mean: my read of the researcher expert

text:
The Fed and Wall Street are fighting the last war. The Suez reopening proves it.

The Fed and the Wall Street hawks calling for more hikes are steering by the rear-view mirror. Look forward and you can see it coming: ships returning to the Suez Canal, oil sliding into surplus, and a container fleet about to swell. 

That is a disinflationary supply shock, and the people setting policy are blind to it.

Start with the canal. The Suez Canal Authority reported 1,490 transits in October and $ 724 million of revenue, the strongest month since the Red Sea crisis began and nearly double a year earlier. 

Container traffic, as charted by Javier Blas at Bloomberg Opinion, has climbed from 20,000 TEU a day through most of 2024 and 2025 to 136,000. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd restore all their Asia-Europe loops to Suez from 4 December.

The Cape detour added two to three weeks a voyage and absorbed 5 to 7 per cent of global container capacity. That capacity is coming back just as the fleet grows 9 per cent in 2027 and the orderbook sits at 45 per cent of existing ships. 

Shanghai to Rotterdam freight is already down 29 per cent from its July peak.

Then add energy. The IEA has the oil market in surplus now and a larger surplus in 2027, with supply up 6.6 million barrels a day. North Sea crude has fallen from $ 136 a barrel in October to about $ 93.

None of this shows up in a New Keynesian model, where growth is inflationary and every strong number demands another hike. The Fed has it backw

Adobe Analytics forecasts nearly $13 billion in online Black Friday sales.

🔸 80%+ plan to manage costs by choosing cheaper gifts or buying for fewer people.
🔸 40% are seeking resale and vintage deals.
🔸 Average holiday budget: $779, down from $796 in 2025.

Bloomberg reports that higher prices, early promotions and spending by wealthier households could lift total sales even as many Americans cut back.

The key distinction: Stronger retail revenues don't necessarily mean stronger consumer purchasing power.

- CW laser products were 80% of the company's total revenue: (60% 70mW, 33–34% 100mW, rest misc). 

- "At present, DSP supply shortages have not been incorporated as a core variable in detailed calculations."

$AAOI is not alone here

en_summary: Asian neoclouds deals with Bytedance/Tencent cancelled due to US export controls, rerouting spare capacity to US players; $CRWV cited 10x demand > supply into 2027 so no compute flooding crash expected. Financing cancellations mean less future competition, good for $NBIS long-term as well-capitalized neoclouds with hyperscaler counterparties win; macro risks like rates impact neoclouds most.
text:
Of course! uhh two things: 

1. Asian neoclouds (eg. Malaysia/Thailand) had their deals cancelled with Bytedance, Tencent etc. due to US export controls. 

So they'll reroute spare capacity back to US players. 

Many are arguing that creates compute flooding, but $CRWV cited 10x demand > supply entering 2027. 

So even if supply comes in, I would still see a large demand imbalance, not prices crashing. If anything... pricing has still gone up from some trackers. But we'll see the full effects in the incoming weeks. 

2. Asian Neoclouds had their financing cancelled/paused due to ongoing risks. 

This is more nuanced, it means less compute/competition comes online in the future, which is a good thing for players like $NBIS? 

It might hurt some semi supply chains (not US neoclouds) as seen with some spot prices dropping around GPU/DRAM  procurement. 

But China would need to build out their own compute anyway for their frontier labs so I see a primarily shift in order timing + bifurcated supply chains than aggregate demand falling. 

I see the well capitalized Neoclouds (with hyperscaler counterparties) winning in the long run like $NBIS, but as Elon said with the "other gupplies" there might be some trouble. 

There's still the overall macro risks like rate hikes, financing, etc. where Neoclouds are typically the most impacted

Too many multifaceted variables at play here; but I think Weebius is the best and ends up on top

text:
Now let’s use facts. 

•  Nvidia’s Singapore subsidiary booked roughly $104 billion in revenue in 2025 (and ~$118 billion over the 12 months to January 2026). That is a large figure, but Singapore functions heavily as a billing/invoicing hub. Nvidia has previously stated that actual shipments to Singapore itself were under 2% of total revenue; most products billed there are shipped elsewhere (including some Taiwan and China business routed through the subsidiary).
•  Under Nvidia’s current geographic reporting (by customer headquarters rather than billing location), the United States accounts for roughly 69% of FY2026 revenue (~$216 billion total), Taiwan ~20%, China (incl. Hong Kong) ~9%, and “Other” ~2%. There is no standalone Singapore line that equates to half the business.
•  The restrictions apply to advanced chips destined for those specific countries (with exemptions), not to Nvidia’s global sales. The company has stated that demand continues to far exceed supply and that it expects performance to remain strong while it assesses the new rules.

text:
Let me get this straight: 

Alice Huang does not appear to be a spy for China... 

but she is a hustler working for a company funded by Alibaba, which wanted GPUs... 

in defiance of intended US export control...

and also in defiance of Chinese government directives to use domestic chips and stop using Nvidia chips, yeah?  

Wherein the actions were not technically illegal under US or Chinese law, but went against the known wishes of both governments?

And now we find that Alibaba and most Chinese AI labs other than Deepseek have mostly built their models on distillation of US labs and now that Anthropic has put a stop to it (apparently poisoning the data), the latest Chinese model releases are DOA?

I had earlier said that [Chinese AI labs] should stop distilling, because all they're getting is warmed-over American slop and turning their models into neoliberal shills. A truly indigenous Chinese model pre-trained on real-world human data would be more possible in China (it costs money but would be cheaper than anything US labs could get) and would yield a materially superior model with data not available to US frontier labs - and would give the world an badly-needed AI voice based on a culture distinct from the West.

So what actually happened here is that Alice Huang harmed *China* by facilitating Chinese AI lab dependence on US chips, and also caused the US to trip up a bit by getting Jensen fired for a week and creating yet another tiresome political fault line.

en_summary: Does a $VIX spike mean buy? Discusses academic evidence, rebuttals and conclusion on whether expected equity returns step up after fear gauge spikes.
text:
https://www.atlaspeakresearch.com/backtests/peak-vix/

DOES A $VIX SPIKE MEAN BUY? THE ACADEMIC EVIDENCE, THE REBUTTALS, AND A CONCLUSION

THE CLAIM

The folk version says buy when the fear gauge screams. The academic version is narrower and more interesting: expected equity returns step up, nonlinearly, after implied volatility reaches extreme levels, and the step-up is large enough to measure years of data at a time. Both versions circulate every time the VIX prints 30 or 35. They are not the same claim, and the literature supports them very differently.

THE EVIDENCE FOR

• Ronn and Xu (Econometrics, 2025) test the folk version directly. Across 29 historical episodes in which the VIX exceeded 30, a strategy of cutting equity exposure above 30 and buying back when volatility subsided underperformed simply holding through the episodes by 10.9% a year. Subsequent S&P 500 returns rose with the level of the VIX. Their conclusion for investors with a high appetite for risk: when the VIX is high, invest, because on average you will be compensated.

• Bansal and Stivers (Financial Management, 2025), over 1990 to 2023, find the equity premium steps up appreciably when the VIX exceeds a threshold around its 80th to 85th percentile, with predictive adjusted R-squared of about 19% at six months and 29% at twelve months, robust across subperiods and out of sample. The relationship is a step, not a slope: below the threshold there is little to harvest, above it the premium jumps.
